{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-nc-c","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"f70602de2d64054b3365af18bb6982275724a500cac217906a592280b47c7e24","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-nc-class-c:lineage:50","source_registry_sha256":"e128656a3d00ba5437556728ebd87f5842c83601163739613417fe77cf9f423b","source_liveness_sha256":"dbfdf3e6d892a41c42c05809a9213d44a78aedd480dc6de23937c97292428b74"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Hazardous driving conditions","heading":"C — Work zones, night driving, sun glare, rain and hydroplaning, flooded roads, wipers and headlights, fog, snow and ice, and wildlife (North Carolina)","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Work zones, night driving, sun glare, rain and hydroplaning, flooded roads, wipers and headlights, fog, snow and ice, and wildlife (North Carolina)
Knowledge domain: how North Carolina marks and enforces highway work zones, the headlight law and night-driving habits, and how to handle glare, rain, hydroplaning, flooded roads, fog, snow, ice and wildlife on the road.

FACT_ID: sec12-F01 | anchor: A01
Driving faster than the posted speed limit inside a highway work zone is unlawful. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec12-F02 | anchor: A01
A highway work zone runs from the first sign marking where the zone begins to the last sign marking where it ends. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec12-F03 | anchor: A01
If a sign at the start of a work zone lists a speeding penalty, that penalty is added on top of any other penalty for the speeding conviction. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec12-F04 | anchor: A01
Orange signs with black lettering are used only to identify work zones, both on the approach and inside the zone. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec12-F05 | anchor: A01
A Flagger sign means a worker in an orange vest ahead is directing traffic with a STOP and SLOW paddle, so stay alert and be ready to stop. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec12-F06 | anchor: A02
Black-on-orange advance signs may tell you to act, such as moving to another lane, and they give that message early enough that you should not wait until the last moment. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec12-F07 | anchor: A02
In work zones, going slower than the traffic around you is a leading cause of rear-end collisions, because confined lanes may leave no escape route. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec12-F08 | anchor: A02
Barricades, cones, drums and flaggers are the traffic control devices used to guide drivers safely through a work zone. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec12-F09 | anchor: A02
North Carolina law requires headlights from sunset to sunrise and whenever you cannot see more than 400 feet ahead. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec12-F10 | anchor: A02
At night use low beams in the city, and on the open road use high beams except when approaching or following another vehicle. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec12-F11 | anchor: A02
Night driving is riskier because visibility is lower, more impaired and tired drivers are out, and oncoming headlights can blind you. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec12-F12 | anchor: A02
If an oncoming driver keeps high beams on, blink your high beams once as a reminder; if they still do not dim, stay on low beam. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec12-F13 | anchor: A02
To avoid headlight glare at night, slow down and look slightly toward the right edge of the road instead of into oncoming lights. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec12-F14 | anchor: A02
Never drive so fast at night that you could not stop within the stretch of road you can actually see. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec12-F15 | anchor: A02
When parked on or beside a highway at night, turn on the emergency flashers and switch off the headlights so they do not blind oncoming drivers. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec12-F16 | anchor: A03
For sun glare, lower the visor and wear sunglasses; if that is not enough, pull off to the roadside until you can drive safely. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec12-F17 | anchor: A03
In rain you must use your headlights and wipers, and you should drive more slowly than normal. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec12-F18 | anchor: A03
Stopping on slippery pavement can take from 2 to 10 times as far as on dry pavement, so allow at least double the usual following distance. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec12-F19 | anchor: A03
Roads are slickest in the first 10 to 15 minutes of rain, when water mixes with oil, dirt, dust and rubber on the surface. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec12-F20 | anchor: A03
On wet pavement drive at least 5 to 10 mph slower than you would on dry pavement. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec12-F21 | anchor: A03
Hydroplaning happens when a thin layer of water lifts the tires off the road, and it can begin at speeds as low as 30 mph in water just over 1/8 inch deep. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec12-F22 | anchor: A03
If you hydroplane, lift your foot off the gas, do not brake, keep the wheel straight and let the car slow until the tires grip again. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec12-F23 | anchor: A03
Deep, open tire tread helps prevent hydroplaning, while worn or under-inflated tires raise the risk; for skid handling, tire pressure on the high side of the maker's range is better. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec12-F24 | anchor: A03
Signs of standing water include reflections on the surface, dimples from raindrops, a slushing tire sound and a loose feel in the steering. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec12-F25 | anchor: A03
Puddles left by rain can cause hydroplaning for hours or even days after the rain stops. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec12-F26 | anchor: A03
Never use cruise control during or after rain, because the time spent switching it off in a hydroplane could cost you control. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec12-F27 | anchor: A04
Since 1970, inland flooding has caused 85 percent of tropical-weather deaths in North Carolina, and half of those involved people driving onto roads known to be flooded. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0075]

FACT_ID: sec12-F28 | anchor: A04
Never drive through standing water on a road, since it may be deeper than it looks and part of the road may be washed out. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0075]

FACT_ID: sec12-F29 | anchor: A04
About 6 inches of fast-moving water can sweep a car off the road, and about 12 inches can float it or roll it over. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0075]

FACT_ID: sec12-F30 | anchor: A04
North Carolina requires every driver to turn on headlights whenever the windshield wipers are in use because of bad weather. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0075]

FACT_ID: sec12-F31 | anchor: A04
If fog is so thick you can barely see, pull well off the road, stop, secure the car, turn on the flashers, exit on the passenger side and stay away from the road. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0075]

FACT_ID: sec12-F32 | anchor: A04
If you must drive in fog, use low beams, slow down, watch for the taillights ahead and keep an eye on vehicles behind you. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0075]

FACT_ID: sec12-F33 | anchor: A04
Bridges, overpasses and shady spots are often the first places to freeze as temperatures fall. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0075]

FACT_ID: sec12-F34 | anchor: A04
In a snowstorm, slow down and use wipers and low beams; cut speed by more than half on packed snow and slow to a crawl on ice. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0075]

FACT_ID: sec12-F35 | anchor: A04
On snow or ice, speed up gently, test your steering and braking feel, and in a manual car start in second gear or higher with a slow clutch release. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0075]

FACT_ID: sec12-F36 | anchor: A04
Allow at least 3 times the normal stopping distance on snow or ice, and when stopping keep off the brake so the engine slows the car. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0075]

FACT_ID: sec12-F37 | anchor: A05
Chains and snow tires can still slide on ice and packed snow, so you cannot start, stop or steer quickly in those conditions. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0076]

FACT_ID: sec12-F38 | anchor: A05
Wildlife collisions can be reduced by slowing down and scanning road edges, especially at dawn, dusk and into the night. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0076]

FACT_ID: sec12-F39 | anchor: A05
Slower speed improves survival for both deer and driver: a deer hit at 35 mph is far less likely to be fatal than one hit at 55 mph or more. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0076]

FACT_ID: sec12-F40 | anchor: A05
Animals are most active at dawn, at dusk and in the first few hours after dark, and spring and fall migrations call for extra caution. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0076]

FACT_ID: sec12-F41 | anchor: A05
Use high beams only when there is no oncoming traffic and no animal right ahead, since bright lights can freeze some animals in place. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0076]

FACT_ID: sec12-F42 | anchor: A05
Many animals such as deer travel in groups, so after seeing one, expect others to follow close behind. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0076]

FACT_ID: sec12-F43 | anchor: A05
When an animal is in the roadway, hold your lane and brake firmly to stop if you can; a short honk of the horn is also an option. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0076]

Misconceptions: braking during a hydroplane makes the skid worse, so ease off the gas instead; driving slowly is not always safest in a work zone, since slower-than-traffic driving causes rear-end crashes; water over a road is often deeper than it looks; chains and snow tires do not make ice safe; fog and snowstorms call for low beams, not high beams; one deer usually means more are near.
Mnemonics: orange means work zone; wipers on, lights on; off the gas, hands straight, no brakes for a hydroplane; standing water on the road means find another way.
Glossary: work zone means the stretch between the first and last work zone signs; flagger means a vested worker directing traffic with a paddle; hydroplaning means tires riding on a film of water instead of the road; low beams means dipped headlights for city, fog and snow; eye shine means light reflected from an animal's eyes at the road edge.
Dynamic facts: work zone penalty amounts are posted on site and are not printed in the handbook, so they are not stated here.
